Two Silent Killers, One Overlooked Crisis:
Malaria & Diarrhoea in Children Under Five

A data-driven examination of how malaria and diarrhoeal deaths cluster among young children across 192 countries — and why addressing them together is essential to reducing child mortality.

Simon Boakye  — MScGH (C), BPH · 25 January 2026 · Gapminder Data, 2020

Overview

Each year, hundreds of thousands of children aged 1–59 months die from two largely preventable diseases: malaria and diarrhoea. This analysis examines where those deaths are concentrated, how the two burdens relate to one another, and what the patterns imply for global health policy.

Using 2020 Gapminder data covering 192 countries, the report analyses geographic patterns in child mortality from malaria and diarrhoeal disease using world maps and a scatterplot. Of the 192 countries in the dataset, 63 had complete data for both indicators in 2020 — the subset used for the correlation analysis.

192Countriesin the full dataset (2000–2021)
63Countrieswith data for both indicators in 2020
183KMalaria DeathsIn Nigeria alone (2020)
134KDiarrhoeal DeathsIn Nigeria alone (2020)

Data & Methods

Two datasets from Gapminder were used: malaria deaths and diarrhoeal deaths in children aged 1–59 months, covering 192 countries from 2000 to 2021. The analysis is restricted to 2020 to enable a consistent cross-country comparison. Both indicators exhibited strong right-skew; values were log-transformed where appropriate. World maps were produced using a logarithmic colour scale, and a scatterplot with a linear regression fit was used to assess the association between the two indicators.

Malaria Deaths in Children Aged 1–59 Months

The geographic distribution of malaria mortality is stark. The burden is almost entirely concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), where most countries carry the highest death tolls. Countries outside the continent report negligible numbers by comparison, underscoring malaria's strongly regional character.

Diarrhoeal Deaths in Children Aged 1–59 Months

The diarrhoeal burden shares some geographic overlap with malaria — sub-Saharan Africa registers high mortality — but differs in an important respect: South Asia, particularly India and Pakistan, contributes very large absolute burdens. This reflects the combined influence of population size and persistent challenges in access to safe water and sanitation.

The Relationship Between the Two Indicators

To assess the association between malaria and diarrhoeal deaths, a scatterplot was produced across the 63 countries with complete data for both indicators. Both axes use a logarithmic scale; a linear regression fit with a 95% confidence band is shown.

Pearson Correlation (log-transformed)  ·  n = 63 countries

r = 0.66

A moderate-to-strong positive correlation: countries with a higher malaria burden consistently also report higher diarrhoeal deaths, pointing to shared structural risk factors rather than coincidence.

Figure 3. Scatterplot of malaria deaths versus diarrhoeal deaths in children aged 1–59 months across 63 countries (2020). Both axes are on a logarithmic scale. The line represents the linear regression fit (Pearson r = 0.66, n = 63); the shaded band shows the 95% confidence interval.

The positive correlation (r = 0.66) is both statistically meaningful and epidemiologically plausible. Countries characterised by weak health systems, poor sanitation, limited access to clean water, and high levels of poverty are simultaneously exposed to malaria transmission and to the conditions that facilitate diarrhoeal disease. The co-occurrence of these two burdens reflects shared structural vulnerabilities, not independent disease dynamics.

Conclusion & Recommendations

Malaria and diarrhoeal deaths frequently co-occur, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa, where most of the global malaria burden is concentrated. The moderate-to-strong correlation between the two indicators underscores that they share common root causes: poverty, inadequate sanitation, limited access to safe water, and under-resourced health systems.

While the malaria burden remains almost exclusively sub-Saharan, diarrhoeal disease also imposes substantial burdens in South Asia — particularly in densely populated countries such as India and Pakistan. This geographic distinction matters for how interventions are prioritised and designed.

Recommendations

  • Direct resources to high-burden hotspots — Nigeria, DR Congo, Niger, Mozambique, Burkina Faso, India, and Pakistan — which collectively drive a disproportionate share of global child mortality from both diseases.
  • Adopt integrated child health strategies that address malaria and diarrhoeal disease concurrently, rather than through separate vertical programmes, to maximise impact and efficiency.
  • Invest in the shared structural determinants: poverty reduction, expansion of safe water access, improved sanitation, and strengthened community-level primary care.
  • Strengthen vital registration and disease surveillance systems to close data gaps — only 63 of 192 countries had complete data for both indicators in 2020 — and enable more precise targeting of interventions.

Data Note

Data sourced from Gapminder (gapminder.org). Indicators: malaria deaths and diarrhoeal deaths in children aged 1–59 months, 192 countries, 2000–2021. Analysis restricted to 2020. Values log-transformed to address right-skew. Pearson correlation computed on 63 countries with complete data for both indicators.
